pairs.subject: module-design
pairs.evidence: crates/core/src/datasets.rs:781 The derived-chain defaults (3 and 10_000) are written by hand both here and in config.rs:841-842 (DerivedConfig::default), and the doc comment says the constant 'mirrors' the config; no test links the two, so if one is changed the other silently stops matching. That is the information-leakage failure module-depth names.

techniques.evidence: crates/core/src/datasets.rs:781 One default is encoded in two modules with nothing tying them together; a grep found only datasets.rs:781/785 and config.rs:841-842. Also seen: the pass-through chain upsert -> upsert_trusted -> upsert_stamped, which adds one parameter per concern, and pool() at :830, which hands out the pool underneath.

crates/core/src/datasets.rs:1136 The hatch is marked (greppable AssertSqlSafe), enclosed and minimal, but none of the 6 sites in datasets.rs states the invariant that makes it safe (e.g. 'the interpolated text is a constant with no caller input'). Property four is missing.

crates/core/src/datasets.rs:5130 The batch verdict (New/Changed/Unchanged plus the revision plan) is a pure function over the state already read; the SQL lives in the driver around it. diff_values, hash_value and simhash are pure too.

crates/core/tests/datasets_batch_equivalence.rs:12 The change classification exists twice (inline at datasets.rs:968 and in plan_chunk at :5142). The two producers are held to one randomized parity test, which is the remedy the technique prescribes.

crates/core/src/datasets.rs:5137 Explicit loop that threads mutable per-key state and produces several outputs (plans and next_revision). The state sequence is the algorithm, so the sequential form is correct here.
crates/core/src/simhash.rs:23 Fingerprinting and diffing are synchronous; async appears only where sqlx I/O happens, so no async colouring leaks into the logic.
crates/core/tests/datasets_bulk_perf.rs:3 The batch-vs-per-record write path is judged by one harness against criteria declared up front (.lanes/criteria.json), not by argument.

pairs.subject: module-design
pairs.evidence: crates/core/src/resilience/store.rs:165 Five AssertSqlSafe(format!(..)) sites in the health store splice SQL constants (SOURCE_COLUMNS_LIST_SQL, RunVerdict::JUDGED_SQL, a correlated-subquery template) into statements. None of them states the fact that makes the splice safe, so an audit of this unverifiable region means investigating each site rather than reading a stated claim.

techniques.evidence: crates/core/src/resilience/store.rs:165 Marked, enclosed in HealthStore, and minimal, but no site carries the invariant (property four). The same holds at :220 and :702/:710.

crates/core/src/resilience/detect.rs:5 The verdict, score and state transition are pure functions; store.rs is the driver, behind the storage feature. The same split holds in doctor::diagnose(facts), retention::plan_artifact_retention (takes older_than as a parameter, :206) and preview::replay.
crates/core/src/resilience/detect.rs:289 The decision core is synchronous; async exists only in the sqlx-facing store and preview_fleet driver. Removing it costs nothing in the logic.
crates/core/src/resilience/detect.rs:844 The health ladder is written as an explicit match over SourceState, the state-machine case the technique says to keep sequential.

crates/core/src/resilience/store.rs:878 One call hides sketching, baseline, drift, invariant checks, scoring, transition and persistence. Its informal interface (call before writing the batch) is documented at the call. Minor: store() at :822 exposes the HealthStore underneath.

declined.subject: module-design
declined.reason: The context is 25+ sequential .sql migration files with no module interface, seam, generator or flow-control code, so none of the 16 module-design techniques has its precondition met in a way I could anchor. The closest finding is that the SourceState vocabulary is encoded both in the 0020_resilient_extraction.sql:27 CHECK and in resilience/mod.rs SourceState::parse. That is held only implicitly, by resilience tests writing every rung, so it reads as a resilience module-depth observation rather than a verdict on the migrations. I did not grep exhaustively enough to justify a not-applicable verdict.
